analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to sell prescriptions to pharmacies at their average foreign prices for Medicare beneficiaries.
analysis.headline: The bill to cut seniors' drug prices to foreign-price levels was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2001 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force drug makers that sell to the federal government to also sell pharmacies, at the manufacturers' average foreign price, enough of each drug to cover what those pharmacies dispense to Medicare beneficiaries — including hospice patients. Because Americans pay more for the same drugs than buyers in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the UK, the bill's sponsors estimated this would cut many seniors' drug costs by roughly 40%. A manufacturer that refused could be barred from federal contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay out of pocket for prescriptions would gain: the bill would require manufacturers to sell pharmacies, at the foreign-average price, enough of each drug to cover what those pharmacies dispense to Medicare beneficiaries, including hospice patients [S2][S3]. The bill's own findings estimate this would cut many beneficiaries' drug costs by about 40% on average, and say many older Americans pay up to ten times what the manufacturers' most favored U.S. customers pay [S3]. Medicare and taxpayers would also benefit from lower program drug spending [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare beneficiaries who buy their own drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires each participating drug manufacturer to make covered drugs available to pharmacies, in an amount equal to what the pharmacy sells to Medicare beneficiaries, at a price no greater than the manufacturer's average foreign price — the average realized in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the UK

The bill's findings estimate the policy would reduce prescription drug prices for many Medicare beneficiaries by an average of 40 percent, addressing a price gap in which older Americans sometimes pay ten times what the manufacturers' most favored U.S. customers pay
Extends the lower prices to drugs furnished to Medicare beneficiaries enrolled in Medicare-certified hospice programs, aimed at terminally ill patients among the most vulnerable
Enforces compliance by debarment — excluding a noncompliant manufacturer from federal contracting for a period matching the seriousness of the failure
Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to report to Congress annually on whether the law is actually reducing prices, with authority to recommend further changes

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost: they would have to sell to pharmacies, in quantities matching what pharmacies sell to Medicare beneficiaries, at no more than the manufacturer's average price in Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, and the UK — well below the prices they charge most U.S. cash-paying customers [S2][S3]. The bill's findings note manufacturers earned $27.3 billion in profits in 1999 partly from these higher U.S. prices [S3]. A manufacturer that did not comply could be debarred — barred from federal contracts for a period matching the seriousness of the failure [S3].

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism — debarment from federal contracts — only applies to manufacturers that contract with the United States, so a manufacturer could avoid the foreign-price requirement by choosing not to sell covered drugs to the government at all

The bill requires the low price on pharmacy purchases but does not directly cap the retail price a senior pays at the counter; it relies on pharmacies passing the savings through, and an honest supporter would acknowledge some of the margin could be retained by pharmacies instead

Tying U.S. prices to an average across six foreign countries, several of which negotiate prices down through government purchasing power, would cut deeply into manufacturers' U.S. revenue, and the industry would argue this reduces the returns that fund drug research and development

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: seniors who pay cash for prescriptions would get roughly the prices paid in peer countries — an estimated 40% average reduction — while drug makers would give up the part of their U.S. pricing built on charging cash-paying customers far more than their best commercial customers and foreign buyers [S3]. The design has real weaknesses worth acknowledging: enforcement depends on voluntary participation in federal contracts, and the retail pass-through of savings is not guaranteed. But the mechanism is a familiar one — most covered foreign nations already negotiate or cap drug prices through government purchasing power [S3]. On balance the bill would have transferred a substantial share of drug spending from seniors and Medicare to the manufacturers' revenue column, and it died without any of those trade-offs being debated.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Johnson introduced the Prescription Drug Fairness for Seniors Act on April 4, 2001, joined by Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle; its findings cited manufacturers' $27.3 billion in 1999 profits and estimated a 40% average price cut for many Medicare beneficiaries.
The bill cited examples of older Americans paying up to ten times what the manufacturers' most favored U.S. customers — health insurers, HMOs, and the federal government — pay for the same drugs.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, which is the standard first step for tax and health financing legislation.

The action history shows no committee hearings, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote at any point before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003; the sponsor's only later activity was introductory remarks in July 2001.
The bill attracted only three cosponsors, all Senate Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor ever signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: the bill that would have required them to sell to U.S. pharmacies at their lower foreign-average prices never advanced, so they kept charging Medicare beneficiaries the higher U.S. cash prices. Seniors paying for their own prescriptions continued to bear those costs, and Medicare missed the taxpayer savings the bill projected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers who kept U.S. seniors' prices high

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and spoke for it on the Senate floor on three occasions during 2001

for.name: Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill's introduction as co-sponsor in April 2001

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it gained no other support in the Senate

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 4, 2001 and took no recorded action — no hearings, no markup, no report — for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: The prescription drug industry fought foreign-price and government-negotiated pricing proposals throughout the 107th Congress as the bills would cut the prices U.S. cash-paying customers pay

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record; opposition was never put to a vote, so the issue split on party lines only in the bill's thin sponsorship.

industries.note: The bill would tie the price these manufacturers charge U.S. pharmacies for drugs sold to Medicare beneficiaries to their average prices in six foreign countries, and could debar manufacturers that did not comply from federal contracts. Their interest in the bill ran against seniors paying cash prices, since the bill targeted the price gap those prices depend on.

Pharmacies would be able to buy, in volumes matching their Medicare-beneficiary sales, at the lower foreign-average price. The bill required the lower price on pharmacy purchases but relied on retail competition to pass savings to seniors rather than capping the shelf price directly.
